results.title: INTO THE LAND OF EGYPT—16 Where Crocodiles were Gods (Ellesmere Guardian, 11 October 1938)
results.fulltext: into the land of egypt16 where crocodiles were gods t wanted to be moving i wanted to get away from cairo where europeans and egyptians are so kind and so hospitable that you continue to stay on there long after you should have left like dublin cairo is a difficult city to leave because people are so friendly invite you out write letters to you ring you up on the telephone and offer to take you here there and everywhere it requires great strength of mind to leave cairo it would indeed be easy to come to egypt and see nothing except that city however one night when i was reading in bed in the shadow of the pyramids i decided to hire a car tlfe next morning and go to the fayum i thought the fayum would be interesting because i had been reading strabo and herodotus for in the old daysthe first four centuries before christgreek and roman tourists always went to the fayum to see the sacred crocodiles at arsinoe i suppose some pre christian thomas cook advertised them as a sight which no visitor to egypt should miss the crocodiles were kept in a sacred lake in the grounds of the temple of sebek they wore gold earrings and splashed the water with forepaws decorated with jewelled bracelets the visitor was expected to make offerings of fried fish and honey cakes but it is clear from the accounts of ancient writers that the crocodiles would have preferred the visitor himself the priests had a trick of opening the crocodiles mouths without getting hurt stealing up as the animals were asleep in the sun they quickly opened their mouths and injected the fried fish and honey cakes leaping back as the crocodiles jumped angrily into the water it is surprising that none of those cynical greeks ever wrote a dialogue between a sacred crocodile and a sacred cow on the horror of being a god to-day the sacred ponds are dried up and there are vast dusty mounds where the temple stood sometimes natives digging in the earth find the mummy of a crocodile brittle as old wood wrapped in yards of fine linen early in the morning i set out for the fayum the road leaves the pyramids to plunge for forty miles across a blinding desert forty miles of desert are just enough to show you what a desert is like but not enough to fill your heart with despair and weariness the sandy track loses itself on a featureless horizon the sand hills shoulder each other mile after mile here smooth as brown velvet there rippled with the wind as if the tide had just gone out and the sun beats angrily upon this dead land until the eyes grow weary and sore with looking at the burning flatness until any objecta bird the white bones of a camel the chassis of a burnt-out ford car comes as a welcome relief from the monotonous sterility one feature of the desert is beauti by h v morton ful the dry clean air it is like the air on top of ben nevis and when you have lived in an eastern city for some time where the air is full of all sorts of things the desert air blowing over thousands of miles of clean sand stirs up the bloodstream and cheers the heart still what a joy it is to see far off the first glimpse of palm trees and to know that in a short time you will enter the first patch of shade hear the gurgle of running water and listen with delight to the sound of birds the fayum is an oasis lying about 140 feet below the level of the mediterranean the arabs say that it was made fertile by the vizier yusuf who caused canals to be dug which brought water and life to the desert the vizier yusuf is the joseph of the bible the track led downhill towards a scene that looked to me like a child impression of the garden of eden the desert ended suddenly against a wall of date palms high up where the fronds spray upwards against the blue sky i saw bunches of date lying like a swarm of bees in heavy clusters the colour of spanish mahogany instead of the barren sand the road now lay along a high embankment of black earth the rich pregnant black earth of egypt and on either side ran slow canals of fresh waterthe veins that carry the life blood of this land the richness of the fayum was proverbial in the days of the pharaohs it was a land with the climate of paradise and to-day it is farmed by the rich landowners of egypt some of whom even know their own farms by sight and attend to the details lof farm management the earth produces almost anything that is sown in it oranges bananas mandarins dates sugar-cane rice maize and the only real crop of olives grown in egypt i the strangest of all the fayum products are sea fish how can sea fish come from an oasis in the desert 150 miles from the sea the answer is that the water of lake karoun a salt lake on the western boundary is chemically much the same as the mediterranean sea how hard the fellah works with what unremitting toil must he slave at this black land giving his life in return for its fruitfulness every head of maize is literally won at the cost of his sweat and the cracking of his muscles he stands to the waist in water his single thin garment drenched with the drip of the shaduf he stands in the clinging mud of the fields the soles of his bare feet making him an easy victim to the terrible germ that lives in the soil of egypt he stands bowed above his virginian plough he strides like pharaoh soldiers on a temple wall slashing at the man-high maize stalks he staggers covered like a jack-in-the green burdened with a load of bersim every day year in and year out century after century it is the same he is the fellah the man whose sweat built the pyramids and the temples the man whose indomitable sense of fatality is perhaps the most colossal of egypt monuments as i pass his pretty villages built in groves of date palms beside shallow canals i smell the wood smoke rising from the ovens where his women are baking the tough bread which is his staple food i see the little mud houses where he goes home to sleep for a few hours before the sun like a trumpet in the morning calls him out to strive again with water and with mud and there is little inside his house of four walls of mud except little children playing in the dust but the fellah is asleep in the wide and comfortable arms of ignorance over 85 per cent of the population of egypt is unable to read and who looking around at the fruits of so-called knowledge to-day would wish to awaken the fellah from his ancient slumber i travelled through the villages to the edge of lake karoun where a small two-storey hotel kept by a young german stands within a few yards of the water edge the hotel was empty because it was mid-week at the week-ends it is filled with sportsmen from cairo who come to shoot the countless thousands of wild duck snipe and teal which haunt the lake-side and i thought that this lake was the most beautiful thing i had seen so far in egypt it is a sheet of blue water lying in the sunlight with the tawny desert on its western shores a desert in which lie forgotten cities of the greek age and old temples falling into dust a few poor fishermen row about the lake with their nets and sell their catches on the shore in the still hush of this remote place the blend of blue water and desert hills i was reminded of another lakethe lake of galilee an arab servant took my bag up to a little bedroom overlooking the lake the bed was covered with a mosquito net and the room smelt cleanly of camphor i have just opened the hotel said young mr schumacher the proprietor for i keep it shut until the shooting season opens what a business it is opening a hotel that has been shut for an egyptian summer the lizards the snakes the birds and the frogs come and live here also the wild bees i knew that i was going to like karoun

results.fulltext: into the land of egypt24 south to aswan t have twice seen the imperial airways seaplane homeward bound from south africa flying low over the desolate valley of the kings so that its passengers might see where tut-ankh-amen is buried although we are now so accustomed to the signt of aircraft in the desert for the largest aeroplane no longer excites the least sophisticated bedouin this machine roaring above the tombs of the pharaohs gave me a momentary thrill what an amazing glimpse its passengers must have as they look down into the yellow furnace of hills once a week the companion flyingboat on its outward journey to south africa comes down on the nile at luxor where it spends a night moored opposite the winter palace hotel on such occasions the whole town gathers on the banks of the nile the seaplane arrives just before sunset after circling luxor it turns and makes a bee-line for the nile descending lower and lower until its floats cut the water and then the immense thing ceases to be a creature of the air and settles heavily like a gigantic water-fowl its engines race as it taxies round to its mooring place making so great a noise that the hawks fly up and circle indignantly in the air a motor-boat explodes out to it a little door in the flying-boat opens almost on the water-line and from the body of the monster step the passengers who come ashore through a crowd of donkey boys dragomans and visitors then the pilots land two fairhaired englishmen in khaki shorts and tunics they stride slowly up the broad steps to the hotel terrace like a couple of roman emperors one morning i rose even earlier than usual because i was catching the train to aswan the sun was rising when i looked across the nile to the libyan hills i saw the first sun rays touching their summits gilding them with a redgold flush while their flanks the colour of dull sand were still streaked with the shadows of night suddenly the morning sileiice was cut by a furious sound the roar of the seaplane taking off from the nile the noise increased as the flyingboat raced upstream churning the mirror-like water into blue wavest i watched for that moment when a space would toe visible between boat and waterthe exciting moment of taking-off slowly the seaplane rose in the air and flew away into the morning sky heading for khartum and the south as i sat in the train to aswan i thought that among the marvels of thebes this flying boat takes a high place to us tut-ankh-amen tomb is wonderful because it opens the gate of the past but what would this pharaoh have said could he have seen the day when two yellow-haired young men with bare knees would guide a ship through the air above the ruins of hundred-gated thebes from luxor to aswan the journey takes five and a half hours and the distance is 129 miles aswan on the borders of the sudan lies in a perpetual sun bath the heat glitters ands trembles over the rocks even in winter time the famous barrage which regulates the supply of nile water and causes egypt to be no longer entirely dependent on the annual nile flood is of course the greatest sight to be seen there but in the town of aswan itself there is nothing but a native bazaar i palm trees desert and one of the largest an3 best run hotels in the world it is built high up overlooking the cataracts where the nile comes rushing down over gigantic rocks of red granite which lie half submerged like a herd of elephants taking a bath in the good days before the war aswan was the resort of people so rich that they considered sight-seeing vulgar and middle-class or of people who combined great wealth with defective bronchial tubes or torpid livers such visitors recognised in the cataract hotel the perfect place in which to do nothing but lie in the by h v morton sun surrounded by countless dark silent servants even in these changed days it is practicalljtmpossible to light your own cigarette in the hotel you may get as far as bringing out a matchbox or even if you are quick you may produce the match but always before you strike it someone glides from a group of lounge palms and jwith a swift conjuring motion lights jyour cigarette y i so instinctive is this hotel respect i for that kind of traveller who is rapidly becoming extinct that when you arrive wearing a battered flitstained sun-hat and an atrocious1 pair of old j flannel trousers the whole place igenufects taking its time from two j small berberine boys who go down lon their knees and wife feather brushes bend reverently over your tomib-torn shoes the age has not yet gone byat least in aswanwhen any beggar may be a wandering god i enjoyed the luxury of this fantastic hotel if the late mr arnold bennett had written about the internal economy of hotels such as this instead of an hotel in a great city where everything is ready in the markets what an interesting book he might have produced it was amusing to watch one of the guests pouting over the sole bonne femme all the way from alexandria on ice and casually as if he were in piccadilly ordering a bottle of liebfraumilch 1921 from a wine waiter imported from switzerland to the sudan border for this purpose i there is something improbable and rather roman about these ritzes and berkeleys planted in the desert neither cicero nor cleopatra would feel out of place as a guest ruins whose marble columns ana chips of porphyry strew the sands from antioch northward through asia minor and southward into egypt were once places like this i think providing the same amazing contrast to their surroundings expressing an alien culture and a different standard of civilisation they also offer a fine example of man victory over circumstances and they all probably shared the same air of impermanence for the first time since i came to egypt the heat almost defeated me when i looked from the cool safety of the terrace out to the white blaze of afternoon light i wanted nothing more than a cold bath a fresh suit of white clothes and a basket chair in the shade driven out however by the feeling that i might never see aswan again i walked slowly through the bazaar where for the first time the traveller smells the sudan i went into a curio shop in which a large sudanese presides1 over an incredible assortment of stuffed crocodiles knives with crocodile skin sheaths tom-toms scimitars ostrich eggs and all sorts of barbaric ornaments the bazaar is untouched by western influences it is partly roofed to keep out the sun and in the hot darkness of the crowded lanes where men and donkeys move in a jostling stream the craftsmen sit at work in their little shops making shoes sew ing clothes hammering metal a crowd in which i noticed a fair percentage of sudanese and a few wildlooking bisharin lean and pantherlike with towering masses of frizzy golliwog hair after dinner that night when 1 was sitting on the terrace watching the moonlight on the i lie an englishman sat next to me and we began talking i asked if crocodiles were still shot at aswan you dont see them nowadays until you go into the sudan he replied where the steamers blow their sirens so that passengers can watch the crocodiles suddenly wake up on the rocks and dive into the river then he told me a good story which he said was true a man came to aswan determined to shoot a crocodile of course he soon found a guide who promised to get him a crocodile for 10 they went out for two days but had no luck on the third day however the sportsman came back to the hotel a mixture of excitement and sorrow saying that they had crawled about on the river banks and among the rocks all day when suddenly they saw a crocodile sunning himself on a rock he took aim and fired the crocodile gave a leap andfell into the river they searched for it in vain the guide soothed his patron and swore to him that this always happened in a day or perhaps two he said the dead crocodile would be washed ashore and he would bring it to the hotel and claim his 10 sure enough he turned up one day with an evil-smelling crocodile received his 10 and the sportsman now in his seventh heaven rushed off to have the beast stuffed before it was too late but it transpired that this was an old trick of the guides he and an accomplice possessed a stuffed crocodile which they were in the habit of putting out on a rock ready for any sportsman who hired their services while the guide having whetted his patron appetite by two days of failure led him within sight of his prey and excitedly told him to shoot the accomplice careful hidden from view pulled a string at the sound of the shot so that the stuffed crocodile fell into the water from which it was carefully retrieved and put away for the next sportsman in the meantime the guides had telegraphed to friends in the sudan where crocodiles really can be shot ordering a crocodile to be sent post haste to aswan and this was the corpse slightly the worse for wear which was delivered in return for 10 could the desire to please go farther i asked ah it wonderful what tricks these fellows will get up to replied my acquaintance

results.title: Plan to guard notorious Israeli prison with crocodiles stalled over animal welfare concerns
results.description: A legal battle has erupted in Israel over a government plan to build a moat around a prison and fill it with crocodiles.
results.fulltext: By Matthew Doran, ABC A legal battle has erupted in Israel over a government plan to build a moat around a prison and fill it with crocodiles. The plan, first proposed by the country's far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir late last year, had largely flown under the radar in recent months until an animal welfare group launched a challenge. On Sunday, local time, the Jerusalem District Court announced a temporary injunction preventing the Israel Prison Service (IPS) from deploying Nile crocodiles to the notorious Ketziot Prison. The facility is in a remote part of the Negev Desert, close to the Egyptian border in Israel's south, and houses many Palestinian prisoners, including some who were involved in Hamas's deadly 7 October 2023 attacks against Israel. Soon after the injunction was ordered, Ben-Gvir took to social media to accuse the Israeli courts of siding with terrorists. Last December, Israel's Channel 13 reported Ben-Gvir, who has responsibility for Israel's prison system, had proposed building a new prison surrounded by a moat filled with crocodiles to deter attempted breakouts. Local media immediately drew parallels with the so-called "Alligator Alcatraz" facility in the United States - an immigration detention centre built in the Florida Everglades and surrounded by wetlands which were home to, among other things, alligators. During a tour of the facility in July 2025, Trump said there were "a lot of cops in the form of alligators" surrounding the site, discouraging escapees. The Florida detention centre was closed and emptied by June 2026. In January, there were further reports and photos that staff from the Israel Prison Service (IPS) had visited a crocodile farm in Hamat Gader, in the southern part of the occupied Golan Heights. The manager of the site, Yosi Mousanejad, told Israel's public broadcaster KAN that he was not going to supply crocodiles to the IPS, and had only been educating their staff. "I'm not putting up crocodiles for security," he reportedly said. "Our crocodiles don't have a security guard hat. We're a tourist farm." That prompted disbelief among an animal rights group, Let the Animals Live, which is now challenging the plan. "We all really laughed here, it was kind of a joke," lawyer Hagit Gluska told the ABC. "We were certain that this is some kind of thing for the election that is coming in Israel." The election has since been set for 27 October. Soon after the photos from the crocodile farm went public, it became apparent that the idea would be applied to the existing Ketziot Prison - a sprawling 400,000 square metre facility housing thousands of Palestinian prisoners. The prison - which is where members of the intercepted Global Sumud Flotilla, including Swedish activist Greta Thunberg and several Australians, were taken before their deportation - has repeatedly come under fire for mistreating prisoners. The detained Australians complained of assault at the hands of Israeli officials - claims which were denied. Israeli human rights organisations have also documented severe mistreatment of Palestinian prisoners, including beatings and sexual abuse. This is where the court case comes from. Last month, Israel's Environmental Protection Minister Idit Silman suddenly declared she had reclassified Nile crocodiles from being a "protected species" to being "cultivated animals" - a change which could allow crocodiles to be used in a place like a prison. The reclassification reportedly ignored the advice of officials within the agencies for which she has responsibility - including the Nature and Parks Authority. When Silman made her ruling, Ben-Gvir reposted an AI-generated image of himself patting a crocodile, with a leash around its neck. "The terrorists' new nightmare," the post read. "Damn terrorist, thinking of trying to escape? Think again." Digging for the moat got underway shortly after the crocodiles were reclassified, and 21 million shekels (NZ$11.8 million) were set aside for the project, the Times of Israel reported. Let the Animals Live appealed to the courts to tear up Silman's ministerial declaration. The group said the reclassification had been done improperly and argued using crocodiles at the prison could cause the animals to suffer. That led to the injunction being handed down, temporarily blocking crocodiles being transferred to the prison until a final court ruling is made. The court gave the Israeli government and the IPS until 16 August to respond to the case. Ben-Gvir was outraged by the intervention, which interrupted his publicly declared push to make conditions in prisons even more extreme for those behind bars - particularly Palestinians. "Once again the legal system is on the side of the terrorists and against the people of Israel," he posted on social media. It is a familiar refrain by the national security minister, who has several convictions for terrorism offences against his name and is subject to sanctions by countries including Australia. In recent years he has joined with other right-wing members of the Netanyahu coalition government to repeatedly accuse the nation's court system of standing in the way of its agenda, and demanded reforms to limit the oversight of the judiciary. On Monday, Ben-Gvir criticised the judiciary again while attending a hearing in the Supreme Court on another matter: a challenge to the government's ban of the United Nations' Palestinian aid agency UNRWA. "There is no limit to the court's intervention," he said while walking through the building. "Yesterday they intervened over not placing crocodiles near the security prisons. Today they want to intervene in the UNRWA law, the day before yesterday it was the judicial reform. "This must be stopped. In the next elections it is a judicial reform or no government." The next day, he posted a video of himself and Silman at Ketziot standing over the channels being dug for the crocodiles. "It is worthwhile being a crocodile with the prison service," Ben-Gvir said. "This is a very clear and explicit statement to those who slaughtered, murdered and raped in our country - that he who does crimes like these will find himself surrounded by crocodiles," Silman said. Before the injunction was issued, human rights monitors had lashed the "Crocodile Ketziot" proposal. Human Rights Watch was among those to criticise the plan, labelling it "so cartoonishly cruel that it should be laughable". "Unfortunately, it's the latest sign of how normalised cruelty has become inside these facilities," HRW's acting Israel and Palestine researcher Sarah Sanbar said in a post on X. -ABC
